reviews.text:
My beloved budgie received excellent care for a long time.

She was unable to eat on her own and underwent a long and arduous hospital stay.

Even in a situation that was far from optimistic, the doctors never gave up on this little life, continuing treatment diligently until the very end, including force-feeding and IV fluids.

Their sincere attitude and their dedication to the life of this one small bird supported me countless times as a pet owner.

Sadly, my beloved bird crossed the rainbow bridge.

Even so, I cannot express enough gratitude to the doctors who worked so hard to keep her alive, and to the staff who provided such warm support.

The nurses and the reception staff always responded kindly to my daily phone calls to check on her condition. They eased my daily anxieties. I am truly grateful.


When I went to pick up my beloved bird today, he treated me with such warmth and care. He had also meticulously groomed my bird, which allowed me to accept my sadness with a gentle sigh.

Even amidst my immense grief, I felt a sense of relief.

Through this experience, I strongly feel that the value of medical care is not determined solely by the outcome—whether a life could not be saved.

The fact that they never gave up on saving my bird and treated it with such sincerity until the very end—that is what I am most grateful for.

Now, my beloved bird rests peacefully in the cage where it lived for so many years.

Seeing it like that, I am overwhelmed with gratitude towards the doctors and staff, and I felt compelled to write this review.

I am truly glad that I entrusted my precious child to Little Bird.

Thank you so much for supporting my little life for so long.

With heartfelt gratitude.

October 13, 2026, From Picchu's mother
i feel doctor and staff have love and passion for the birds. same as in human doctor, waiting time can be quite long even with reservation. cash payment only.

This is a hospital I've used many times when my pet bird was unwell.

Since it specializes in birds, I understand that it's inevitably crowded, as patients come from all over the place. However, I often see situations where 2-3 people come in for just one bird, occupying the chairs in the small waiting room, and the staff don't seem to say anything, which is frankly annoying. (There are notices posted, though.)

Other than that, I think it's a very good hospital. I look forward to continuing to use their services.

This was my first visit. Thank you so much for thoroughly examining my tiny bird; it was saved from serious injury.

I've decided to use this hospital for future bird care.

This review is not directed at the hospital itself.
It is directed at some pet owners.
As you all know, this place is very small, and the waiting room is sometimes so crowded that there are no seats available. As the sign indicates, only one person is allowed in the waiting room at a time.
Yet, there are quite a few pet owners who come in pairs, both sit down comfortably, and chat away. Meanwhile, there are people standing around holding their birds.
I wish the hospital staff would address these issues. (I understand they are very busy and may not have the time to pay attention to them.)
I am writing this in the hope that it will catch the eye of people searching for reviews and considering visiting this hospital, and that it will help reduce the number of pet owners with poor manners.

I took my budgie chick to the vet because its wing was unnaturally raised. An X-ray revealed a fracture, but since it couldn't be treated, we decided to wait for it to heal naturally.

The clinic was crowded, seemingly fully booked, but the explanation of the diagnosis, advice on care, and answers to my questions were all very thorough.

The phone call for the appointment and the receptionist's service were also excellent.

I have a regular vet nearby, but I would like to visit this clinic again if anything happens.


Addendum:
My budgie was hospitalized for egg binding.

I was grateful that they were able to see it on the same day, as it was a life-threatening condition. However, they wouldn't tell me when it would be discharged unless I asked, and I had to adjust my work schedule to pick it up, only to wait an hour for the examination to finish in about a minute. The doctor then unilaterally talked about estrus suppression, which was a bit upsetting.

This is a trustworthy hospital for bird care.

A 3-week-old Java sparrow chick was on the verge of death due to poor development, but the head veterinarian examined it carefully, explained its condition and treatment plan, and then hospitalized it for treatment, treating it for coccidia and restoring its weakened state.

It miraculously survived another episode of ileus, which we had prepared ourselves for, thanks to the doctor's accurate diagnosis and early treatment.

The head veterinarian may seem reserved and difficult to talk to, but he explains things clearly regarding the bird's health and care, so I recommend asking him questions.

The young female veterinarian also provides accurate diagnoses and prescriptions based on evidence-based medicine (EBM) and research papers.

I think it's best to consult a veterinarian who has actually seen and handled your bird rather than relying solely on the internet for information on your pet bird's health (considering individual differences).

The fact that there are many experienced bird owners here is surely a reflection of the trust they have in the doctor and the hospital.

(Addendum) The nurses are kind and will quickly take in birds that are particularly ill. However, it can be difficult to get through on the phone, and consultation times can be delayed, resulting in long waits. The waiting room is small with limited seating, and only one accompanying person is allowed. Payment is cash only.

I accidentally clipped my 5.5-year-old male budgie's nails, but I think I pressed too hard and hurt his toes. He looked like he was in pain, so I called in a panic to make an appointment.

The doctor who examined me was a young man, and he explained things clearly, was calm, and made a good impression. He listened carefully and handled everything from restraints to weight measurements and fecal examinations efficiently. You could sense his love for birds from his demeanor. I was grateful for the appropriate guidance and information he provided me with. (Many pet care methods have advanced, and my knowledge, which was from the Showa era, has been greatly updated.)


Appointments are required, and the clinic is busy, but the receptionist listens to your symptoms and passes them on to the doctor first, so the examination proceeds efficiently. However, I personally don't like describing my parakeet's symptoms at the reception desk, where more than 10 people waiting can hear everything. Fortunately, my bird's symptoms aren't severe, but I'd be a little uncomfortable talking to the receptionist in front of everyone about my seriously ill bird.

・From arrival to departure, it takes at least 45 minutes, and at most an hour and a half.

・Payment is cash only. The register has a retro feel like an antique. Many people say they don't have enough money when paying (lol). The lowest bill starts at around 1,500 yen, but for hospitalization it can run into the tens of thousands of yen. Some people withdraw the money, while others deposit some and pay the rest next time.

・When visiting, you will need a cover or bag to cover your bird's cage. The first time, I went in with it bare, which was a mistake.

My bird was X-rayed, and I was relieved to find that it wasn't broken. At the same time, it was pointed out that his nose was brown, and (although the owner had been vaguely concerned) a testicular tumor was suspected, so he was prescribed medication and given instructions on a diet (46g at the time!).
Until then, he'd been fed seed 24 hours a day (!) and even human rice and bread, but we switched to a diet where we measured him daily, fed him the prescribed amount, and then cut him off at night. At about four months old, his weight stabilized at around 37g, and medication helped him regain his blue nasal lump, so we stopped visiting the hospital.

I've also taken him to the hospital when he turned brown, suddenly lost weight (during molting), or suddenly gained weight. He's now six and a half years old, and the tumor hasn't grown, and he's doing well.

(Addendum)
After he turned six, his wax film turned brown again, so we started medication. This time, there was no improvement, and he gradually began spending more time sleeping with his feathers tucked up. He previously wouldn't let me scratch him, but now he does, and he's become quite attached to people. An ultrasound during a visit revealed that the tumor was significantly pressing on his internal organs. Recently, I noticed that he had been feeling unwell, not singing or talking, and after about three months, he passed away one morning in early October 2025. He was 6 years and 9 months old. I am grateful to the doctor for providing me with emotional support during his final days. As an owner, I was prepared for the loss, but I think my beloved bird did a great job despite the tears. I wonder if I will meet him in heaven.

This was a cockatiel.
He passed away three days after being admitted to the hospital. At the time of admission, they said there was a less than 10% chance of him dying.
He had a blood test and the numbers were normal, but they said they didn't know what was causing his illness.
He passed away on the day we were planning to take him home.
The day before, he had no appetite, so I asked if he would eat at home. They said that this can happen sometimes, so I asked if I wanted to discharge him, but they said he wasn't at that stage yet.
What was the treatment policy for him, considering his numbers were normal and the cause was unknown?!
I rushed over to pick him up on the day he passed away, and they asked if I wanted him put in a bag.
Of course I wouldn't put him in a bag.
There are reviews on other sites, so I think you should take a look.

From here on, this is purely my personal opinion, but I wonder if they would have handled it if he had become ill in the middle of the night.
It was a mistake on my part, and I only regret it.

We have three budgies being treated here.

One of them is almost 10 years old, but thanks to the early detection of macrorhabdus, its life was saved. In Tokyo, where there are few specialized bird hospitals, this is a truly invaluable resource. I would choose to live in this area because of Little Bird.

The doctor is a young man, but he is kind and friendly to children. The reception staff are also kind, making it a trustworthy hospital.

[Update]
Our 3-month-old budgie was successfully discharged after a week-long hospital stay. During its hospitalization, they did everything they could, including injections, IV fluids, and liquid food, and its weight recovered from about 20g to 30g. Thank you so much.

It's by appointment only, but it's always crowded, and sometimes so crowded that you can't even find a seat. Be prepared to stand for over an hour in a cramped space.

On my first visit, I was advised to have my bird hospitalized for tests, and after being diagnosed with an illness, I went for regular checkups. However, each time I had to wait a long time, the consultation time was short, the reception staff's attitude was terrible and made me feel very uncomfortable. Since the symptoms didn't improve even with medication, I transferred to another hospital for further testing. It turned out that the medication prescribed here was almost ineffective, and my bird passed away just as we were about to begin treatment. I've regretted ever since that I didn't transfer sooner.

If you don't want to lose your beloved bird, I recommend going to a different hospital.

I go there when my regular hospital (run by a doctor who trained at Little Bird) can't treat my bird's symptoms.
I'm grateful that they're willing to see me even though I only come here when things are really serious.
It's located just a few minutes' walk from Gotokuji Station. You take an old elevator to the entrance, which is at the end of a narrow alleyway typical of Tokyo, and you're right there when you exit.

It's surprising how old the building is, but I trust the doctor, so I go there.

It's true that the doctor can be brusque, and he gives off an air that makes it difficult to ask questions, but I've only ever experienced veterinarians who only brag about their facilities and criticize other doctors for making mistakes when prescribing nutritional supplements, veterinarians who lie about treating birds when they can't, and veterinarians who make nasty remarks about topics unrelated to birds, so I don't mind his brusqueness at all.

In my case, my first cockatiel was bitten on the tongue by a fellow veterinarian and couldn't eat, so he had to be hospitalized. He was hospitalized for two weeks, but thanks to this hospital, he recovered and is doing well.

PS

My second cockatiel, 21 years old, developed cataracts in his left eye and was hospitalized due to the pain, preventing him from eating. To be honest, I had some bad thoughts, but I had no choice but to leave it to the doctor, so I admitted him as a last resort and he recovered.

A year later, his right eye also developed cataracts, rendering him completely blind. This time, he was again unable to eat due to the pain, so I hospitalized him and began IV treatment, force-fed him, and after being discharged, they helped him grow to the point where he could eat and drink water on his own, even without his sight.

He refused to drink the medicated water, and I was shocked and stunned when I received a phone call telling me that his weight had dropped from 85 grams to 68 grams, but I trusted him and left him in their care.

After he was discharged from the hospital, both he and I experienced difficulties due to his blindness, but he gradually adapted to his blindness and is living a peaceful life. Even after he lost his sight, I loved him very much and took great care of him. I don't think we could have provided the care we needed at our local hospital. Thank you for saving my precious, irreplaceable bird's life.

PS 2
I made a mistake and developed a nut allergy in my first cockatiel, which required hospitalization and treatment. He was hospitalized for a long time and repeatedly admitted and discharged, but thanks to your accurate diagnosis and treatment, he was able to be safely discharged. I'm truly glad I entrusted him to you. As an aside, I could tell from your caring dedication that your cockatiel had grown so attached to you.

I live in northern Kanto, so it's difficult to commute, but when I think about my birds, this hospital is so reliable that the distance doesn't seem like a problem. Thanks to you, my three precious birds have lived long lives. It's thanks to you that I feel happy having my birds by my side. Thank you so much!

It can be difficult to get through on the phone to make an appointment, but I think that's proof that pet owners from all over the country want to come here. It is reassuring for bird owners to know that there is a doctor who will see them immediately (and make an appointment for the same day) whether it is a first visit or an emergency.

Reservations are required.

Even with a reservation, it's always crowded.

I wonder if it's a little different on weekdays?

I had been taking my beloved bird to this clinic for many years. When my bird was still young, it suddenly became ill, and when no other clinics were open on a holiday, they kindly accepted it as an emergency case on their day off. I've been a patient ever since. The clinic was always busy, but recently, it's become difficult to get through on the phone, and the head veterinarian seems overwhelmed with patients, resulting in less than five minutes of consultation time. They don't answer owners' questions very well, and the atmosphere makes it difficult to even ask questions. I didn't feel like I was getting a proper examination, and I was left with a lingering sense of unease each time.

My bird became elderly, and its health deteriorated. Its condition didn't improve, and I didn't want it to pass away there, so I transferred it to another clinic. Ultimately, it passed away six months later, but I realized how important it is for the owner to feel about their beloved bird's final moments.

The good points are the reasonable fees and the ease of making an appointment if you can get through on the phone. However, the consultation time is short.
